title: From Service to Screen: Post-Production Workflow
summary: A repeatable editorial pipeline for full-length video, audio publishing, photography, and social-first clips.
facts: Editing briefs and reviews
24-bit audio deliverables
Short-form and full-length output
fullCaseHtml:
Producing a live service is only the beginning of the media process. The next challenge is translating one recording into material suited to different audiences and distribution channels.

At Pentecostal Tabernacle, I coordinated recurring editing assignments, set deadlines, provided examples, reviewed work, and helped manage deliverables ranging from full-length program videos and sermon excerpts to audio episodes, event photography, and vertical social clips.

Building a repeatable editorial pipeline

01 / INPUTCapture & organizeRecordings, photos, reference examples, and media handoff

02 / BRIEFSpecify outputsAudience, aspect ratio, format, creative direction, deadline

03 / EDITReview & refineEditors cut, sync, select, polish, and submit working versions

04 / SHIPPublish & archiveVideo platforms, podcast audio, shorts, and organized assets

The goal was to avoid relying on an editor to guess the final use of a recording. A useful production brief should answer four questions: What material are we starting with? What needs to be delivered? Who is it for? When does it need to be ready?

Example: the three-output worship brief

In May 2026, I introduced a repeatable approach to separating worship performances from service recordings. For each selected worship set, my brief requested three specific exports:

RECREATED EDITOR DELIVERABLESMAY 2026

01 / Full-length video

Extract the full musical segment from the service recording, preserving continuity across the performance.

02 / Audio master

Provide a standalone 24-bit WAV file suitable for a separate audio publishing workflow.

03 / Vertical reel

Choose a compelling moment and export a 15–90 second social-first clip.

04 / Delivery

Place the complete output set into the designated shared production folder for review and distribution.

Based on the original editing brief. Original server URLs, access information, and internal contacts are excluded.

Scheduling work and guiding other editors

The structure extended to sermon video editing. In March 2026, for example, my assignment brief specified that an editor should prepare the complete service video, extract the sermon as separate audio and video, and deliver at least one 15–90 second short-form clip. Dates, reference examples, and instructions were included directly in the task.

Other assignments involved editing event photography and syncing externally recorded audio to a filmed service when the camera's audio was unreliable. I also outlined ways to present behind-the-scenes footage together with the main program feed and production communications.

These tasks combine practical technical knowledge with team management: translating a creative request into a clear assignment, organizing handoffs, and giving others the information they need to execute well.

Creative supervision, not credit-taking

My role in many of these assignments was briefing, supervising, and coordinating other editors—not personally editing every deliverable. That distinction matters to me.

A strong media team shouldn't depend on one person doing every technical task. It needs consistent standards and a process where different contributors can deliver work with confidence.

What I took forward

This experience strengthened how I approach multimedia production as a system rather than a series of disconnected files. The same principles apply in educational media: clear learning objectives, reusable templates, manageable deadlines, review checkpoints, and media packaged for the audience and platform.

title: 31st Pastoral Anniversary: Recap Film
summary: Editorial direction and creative briefing for a milestone anniversary recap film.
facts: Creative brief
Editorial supervision
Archival storytelling
fullCaseHtml:
In the spring of 2026, Pentecostal Tabernacle prepared to recognize Bishop Brian Greene's 31st pastoral anniversary. One media component was a recap film drawing on footage from the previous year's anniversary gala.

My role was developing the creative brief, assigning and supervising the edit, and coordinating the production handoff. The editor was responsible for the actual assembly; my job was to communicate the story we wanted to tell and set the editorial direction.

Framing the story

This wasn't intended to be a chronological record of every part of the gala. The brief called for a short video that felt high-energy, tasteful, celebratory, and personally focused on the honoree.

The archival source material also included people presenting awards and offering spoken tributes. I emphasized those recordings as a key part of the story, so that the finished piece would have emotional substance rather than functioning as a silent montage.

RECREATED CREATIVE BRIEFAPRIL 2026

Runtime

Target a concise 2–5 minute recap suitable for use during the anniversary program.

Narrative focus

Center Bishop Brian and the surrounding community, emphasizing joy and celebration.

Editorial foundation

Build from gala footage and incorporate meaningful portions of the recorded presentations and speeches.

Production guidance

Provide visual references, a first-draft deadline, time allocation, and a scheduled creative review.

This is a public-facing reconstruction of the April 15 brief, not an internal production document or claim of personally editing the video.

From brief to delivery

APR 15

Creative direction shared

Assigned the recap, established the story, editorial tone, target length, and review checkpoints.

APR 16

Reference material sent

Provided examples of energetic horizontal and vertical recap formats to guide the editor.

JUN 06

Video handoff

Shared the anniversary reel with the production team and confirmed its planned placement after the offering.

Watch the delivered anniversary reel ↗

What I brought to the project

This project demonstrates a part of production leadership that's easy to overlook: writing a brief that gives an editor enough creative freedom while establishing clear boundaries for the outcome.

I defined what the viewer should feel, which source material mattered most, where the piece would be shown, and how reviews would fit into the timeline. I then supported the transition from an editorial project into a live-event playback asset.

title: Media Team Development & Training
role: Interim Director of Media · Production Lead
summary: Hands-on workshops, onboarding, and peer mentorship to develop production volunteers.
facts: Four-service onboarding model
Approx. 15 volunteers
11-slide orientation guide
fullCaseHtml:
Working in live production has taught me that the success of a team depends on more than the equipment it uses. The people operating it need opportunities to learn, ask questions, and grow in confidence.

At Pentecostal Tabernacle, I helped lead a volunteer media team supporting weekly services, conferences, and special events. Alongside coordinating technical production, scheduling, and creative projects, I wanted to make it easier for new volunteers to gain the practical skills they needed to contribute.

Training in a live-production environment

One part of that work was developing a four-service, hands-on onboarding program that introduced approximately 15 volunteers to live media production. Instead of relying only on an initial explanation of the equipment, the approach paired new volunteers with experienced operators during actual services.

This gave incoming team members a chance to learn in context: seeing how camera operation, video switching, and live-production responsibilities fit together, while having someone experienced nearby to guide them.

It also gave existing volunteers a meaningful role in developing the next group of operators. That kind of peer-to-peer support was important to how I approached the team.

Inside the orientation guide

The onboarding program was supported by an 11-slide orientation guide introducing the media team's responsibilities, expectations, training opportunities, and day-to-day operations. The material covered production, audio, and social media and communications, so volunteers could see how their work fit into the broader team.

One of the most useful visuals was a shadowing model with four stages marked 0%, 30%, 70%, and 100%. It illustrated a gradual increase in hands-on participation rather than expecting a first-time operator to take over immediately. These percentages describe the training stages shown in the guide, not measured completion rates.

01 · Introduction to the media team

02 · How the production teams fit together

09 · Additional learning opportunities

10 · The four-stage shadowing model

↓ View or download the full 11-slide orientation (PDF)Click any slide to inspect it at a larger size.

Creating opportunities to learn

Beyond regular onboarding, I coordinated a photography workshop on May 9, 2026, facilitated by photographer Wesley Morris, and a camera-operator workshop scheduled for May 14, led by Jeffrey Douyon. Both learning opportunities were organized for volunteers with different levels of experience.

The planning involved more than picking dates. I coordinated volunteer communications, registrations, venue arrangements, instructor coordination, and payment requests so participants and facilitators had what they needed. The photography workshop was also open to PT's social media and partner teams.

A camera-focused production moment from my photography collection.

Supporting volunteers beyond the building

Not every volunteer could attend Thursday rehearsals in Cambridge. In June 2026, I welcomed a volunteer who participated remotely as a livestream content host, sending written guidance, a prepared hosting script, moderation instructions, and a point of contact for technical escalation. That made it possible for someone living out of state to contribute to live digital engagement.

The role had a real operational purpose: facilitating a welcoming conversation during broadcasts, monitoring chat, and responding appropriately when moderation was needed. To make it sustainable, I helped connect the volunteer to team communications rather than depending on individual reminders.

EXAMPLE / REMOTE-VOLUNTEER HANDOFFJUNE 2026

01 / Prepare

Supply a clear hosting script, prompts, and expectations before service.

02 / Equip

Assign chat-moderation access and explain when to remove inappropriate comments.

03 / Support

Provide a designated backup contact for issues during the livestream.

04 / Integrate

Include remote team members in recurring schedules and communications.

Recreated from the volunteer handoff; private email addresses, scripts, and access details are omitted.

Building repeatable production standards

My approach to volunteer development was reinforced by a broader effort to document how the production team worked. For instance, I drafted sermon presentation submission guidelines in October 2024: speakers were asked to send a title, scriptures, and key points three days ahead of their presentation; the media team would return formatted slides the following day, leaving a review window before the event.

This is a small example of instructional design applied to operations. A clear process reduces last-minute ambiguity and helps volunteers and speakers understand what information makes a successful production possible.

T−3Speaker inputTitle, key points, scriptures, and technical needs

T−2Production draftMedia team formats and shares presentation

T−1ReviewCorrections, quality checks, and final handoff

Leadership behind the scenes

The training work was connected to my broader production leadership responsibilities. I coordinated volunteer schedules and assignments, helped prepare teams for services and events, and communicated across production, worship, and creative teams.

That combination of people development and day-to-day production coordination shaped how I approached the role: a team should be prepared for the next service, but its members should also have room to build skills that will serve them beyond it.

Documented scope

  • Approximately 15 volunteers participated in the four-service onboarding program.

  • 11 orientation slides explained production roles, expectations, and the progression from observation to hands-on operation.

  • Two specialist workshop opportunities were coordinated in May 2026, along with ongoing rehearsals and volunteer scheduling.

  • Remote participation extended the team's reach beyond the in-person production crew.

These are program activities and materials, not measured retention or placement outcomes.

What I took from the experience

A well-run production matters, but helping someone become capable of running one is just as meaningful to me. This experience brought together two parts of my work that I want to keep developing: creative and technical production, and teaching and mentoring people.

The four-service onboarding structure and the dedicated workshop opportunities reflect the kind of work I want to keep doing: creating learning experiences while supporting the people who make productions happen.

title: Holy Week Devotional Video Series
summary: An eight-part educational devotional video series developed with a six-person production crew.
facts: 8 videos
6-person crew
27.5k+ initial combined views
fullCaseHtml:
This past Holy Week, I had the privilege of directing a six-person crew to produce an eight-part video devotional series for Pentecostal Tabernacle. We crafted a daily sequence of reflections designed to guide the community through the biggest week in the Christian calendar.

Watch this devotional on YouTube ↗

Pre-Production

This project began with a proposal. It was revised and approved by Pentecostal Tabernacle's creative team and executive board. The scripts would be pre-written by me and approved by the communications director of the church, but we all agreed to let the speaker have some creative liberties. We wanted the content to be emotionally valuable for the talent and feel personal to the congregation, so we made a special effort to pick members of the community who were well-spoken, personable, and represented the diversity of the church.

From the proposal, you can see that we also originally planned to shoot on the streets outside of their south campus, but because of weather changes and consideration of staff and talent, we moved inside the building and pivoted to shots with a heavy focus on the stained glass in the historical building.

For the original production artifacts, cast blocks, and scripts, see the expanded section below.

Inside the original production brief

The campaign document makes the scale and constraints visible. The shoot was scheduled for March 21, 2026, with an 11:00 AM crew call, a 12:00 PM cast call, and a planned filming window of 12:00–2:30 PM at the South campus.

Eight community speakers each received an assigned day and a short, pre-written script. I grouped the shoot into two cast blocks, accommodating performers who needed to arrive later or leave early.

08ORIGINAL EPISODE SCRIPTS

01PLANNED FILMING DAY

27.5k+VIEWS IN FOUR WEEKS

RECREATED CAST / CAMERA PLANMAR 21 · 2026

11:00 AM · Crew call

Prepare the sanctuary location, camera positions, sound, lighting, and room setup.

12:00 PM · First cast block

Palm Sunday, Holy Monday, Holy Saturday, and Holy Wednesday.

1:00 PM · Second cast block

Good Friday, Resurrection Sunday, Holy Tuesday, and Maundy Thursday.

2:30 PM · Planned wrap

Complete coverage and transition the recordings into a one-week post-production schedule.

Recreated from the original shoot schedule. Internal contact details have been omitted.

The original Easter video campaign document contains the full cast plan and all eight scripts.

Original script archive

I wrote eight short, standalone scripts to match the day-by-day publishing sequence. Each focused on a specific event or theme and closed by inviting the community to Easter services. The first production draft appears below for readers who want to inspect the instructional writing behind the videos.

01 / Palm Sunday — Elder Anita Ray

Script context: John 12:12–19 · Cast block: 12:00 PM

7 Days before Jesus Christ was resurrected, he entered into the city with a lot of commotion. This Palm Sunday we remember how Jesus came humbly into Jerusalem on a donkey but was met with the praise fit for a king. We now have the same call to action. Jesus may appear in our lives in an unexpected way but we choose how we respond. Come praise Jesus with us this Easter at Pentecostal Tabernacle right here in Cambridge.

02 / Holy Monday — Joel Holly

Script context: Cleansing the Temple · Cast block: 12:00 PM

6 Days before Jesus Christ was resurrected, He was in the temple disrupting the status quo. “My Temple will be a house of prayer,” He said “but you have turned it into a den of thieves.” It’s encouraging to remember how little Jesus puts up with foolishness in His House but do we carry out the first part of what he said? “My Temple will be a house of prayer,”
Come pray with us this Easter at Pentecostal Tabernacle right here in Cambridge.

03 / Holy Tuesday — Elder Cam Edey

Script context: Mark 12:28–34 · Cast block: 1:00 PM

5 Days before Jesus Christ was resurrected, Jesus shared wisdom and challenged religious leaders. He answered their most important question “ What is the greatest commandment?” Jesus boldly replied: Love God and love others. He didn’t focus on rules for rules sake, but to encourage love. That same challenge still stands for us today.
Come show your neighbor some love this Easter at Pentecostal Tabernacle right here in Cambridge.

04 / Holy Wednesday — Mia Tao

Script context: Mark 14:10–11 · Cast block: 12:00 PM

4 Days before Jesus Christ was resurrected Judas, made a choice that would set the course of history. He went to the religious leaders and agreed to betray Jesus for 30 pieces of silver. Jesus knew the hearts of the people and still moved towards the cross with love and purpose. This Easter, we’re reminded that no matter what challenges or betrayals we face, God’s love never fails.
Come experience His grace with us this Easter at Pentecostal Tabernacle right here in Cambridge.

05 / Maundy Thursday — Tim Joseph

Script context: The Last Supper · Cast block: 1:00 PM

The Day before Jesus Christ was killed he washed his disciples feet at the last supper. The imagery of the last supper is iconic but not the image of Jesus washing his disciples feet. It’s hard to imagine God on his knees washing the feet of his students but It’s an example of how we should serve each other.
Think of some ways you can serve your community this week and come worship with us this Easter at Pentecostal Tabernacle right here in Cambridge.

06 / Good Friday — Anna Adekogbe

Script context: Mark 15:21–39 · Cast block: 1:00 PM

The Day Jesus Christ was killed, what looked like defeat was actually the greatest act of love! He took on sin, pain, and death so we could have freedom. Think of the person you love the most in the world. Could you give your life for their’s? Could you give your life for someone you didn’t love? How about someone who hated you?
Come give thanks for the price Jesus paid with us this Easter at Pentecostal Tabernacle right here in Cambridge.

07 / Holy Saturday — Joyce Holly

Script context: The sealed tomb · Cast block: 12:00 PM

The Day after Jesus was killed, they still conspired against him. A guard was hired to make sure the disciples didn’t come in the night to steal Jesus’ body away. Unknowingly the guard became witnesses of the resurrection. Jesus Christ may have been dead but did not stay dead and there was nothing the devil or anyone else could do about it.
Come celebrate the resurrection and new life with us this Easter at Pentecostal Tabernacle right here in Cambridge.

08 / Resurrection Sunday — Aaron Jennings

Script context: The resurrection · Cast block: 1:00 PM

The Day Jesus Christ was resurrected, death became something you no longer needed to fear. That’s the gospel. Someone loves us so much that he gave His own life to cripple death forever. So now with Jesus in your heart, your sins are forgiven and you are made new. No one could give you a greater gift than this. So what will you do with your new freedom? If you had a blank check, what would you spend it on? And who would you spend it with?
Come rejoice with us this Easter at Pentecostal Tabernacle right here in Cambridge.

Production

We pulled off this very quick job within a single day with PT's stellar media team. With the entire sanctuary to ourselves, we had ample space to create some excellent shots fully utilizing the beauty of the building.

  • Creative Director: Bethel Adekogbe

  • Director of Photography: Susanna Donkor

  • Script Supervisor & Consultant: Erica Kelly

  • Production Sound Mixer: Berlyn Joseph

  • Chief Lighting Technician: Abigail Sah

  • Talent Relations Manager: Anna Adekogbe

  • Lead Production Coordinator: Joshua Ikegwu

▣

Production photographs and background

The original project gallery includes behind-the-scenes images from the sanctuary shoot; the complete public-facing production plan and scripts are archived above.

View the original behind-the-scenes gallery ↗

Post-Production

We filmed everything one week before Holy Week began, so we had to edit everything within a single week! Thankfully, we had such excellent content filmed, so it was easy to edit it into something wonderful. With some light foley work and some color correction, we were able to create an excellent video series that released day by day, celebrating the Easter season.

This campaign gained over 27,500 views in the first four weeks after the initial post.

You can find the entire video series on all Pentecostal Tabernacle's social media, and we've included some written comments from Pentecostal Tabernacle's leadership below.

Watch Easter Sunday devotional on YouTube ↗

Great job on creating the wonderful devotionals this week! — Elder Lady Carmen

Thank you for sharing these videos. They are well done and thought provoking. — Elder Roy Ray

title: Worship Night: Hallelujah
summary: Directed live cameras and coordinated a 12-person production team for a full-scale worship event.
facts: 12-person production team
Live switching
Livestream and edited deliverables
fullCaseHtml:
Worship Night: Hallelujah was a live worship event produced at Pentecostal Tabernacle in Cambridge on November 8, 2025. The event brought together music, stage presentation, and a coordinated technical production to serve both the in-person audience and people watching online.

My responsibilities included directing the video production, switching the live program, and coordinating a 12-person production team. The project brought together camera work, audio/video coordination, photography, and livestreaming in a single high-pressure event.

The finished livestream

Original public livestream, November 8, 2025. Open on YouTube ↗

Preparing a full evening of live content

Worship Night required production teams to coordinate around rehearsals, a detailed music program, performance cues, and changing stage activity. The week before the event included a dress rehearsal intended to run the whole evening from start to finish.

For me, the challenge was translating that preparation into decisions made in real time: choosing shots, communicating across the production team, following the musical flow, and keeping the stream cohesive for people who were not in the room.

01Plan & rehearseConfirm crew roles, camera coverage, program cues, and key musical transitions.

02Direct liveCoordinate video operators, switch the feed, and keep livestream output aligned with the room.

03Deliver mediaSupport photography, full-service recording, highlights, and social-first video outputs.

What I coordinated

RECONSTRUCTED PRODUCTION SYSTEMLIVE EVENT

Camera coverage

Directing camera operators and selecting live framing as performers and speakers moved on stage.

Video switching

Building the program output across multiple camera feeds and prepared event media.

Live audio & communication

Coordinating with technical colleagues so audio, picture, timing, and switching worked together.

Audience-facing delivery

Supporting the livestream, full-event recording, and production assets for additional edits.

Illustrative description of the production system, not a reproduction of PT's internal signal diagram.

A second opportunity: showing the direction process

In August 2026 I also assigned a follow-up editorial concept using the program video, a behind-the-scenes camera, and the production communications recording. The brief asked for synchronized horizontal and vertical edits, a picture-in-picture view of the crew's work, and several short reels highlighting interesting production moments.

That brief captures what makes this event valuable in a professional portfolio. The finished livestream shows the audience experience; a synchronized behind-the-scenes edit would help explain the creative and technical decisions made by the team. The brief is documented, but I am not representing the proposed behind-the-scenes edits as finished or published.

My role and takeaway

This production demonstrates leading people in a live environment: making decisions while multiple departments are active, communicating clearly, and protecting the audience experience throughout a long performance.

It also reflects the production philosophy I continue to use: support skilled operators with a strong plan, then give them the direction and trust they need to execute it.

title: Easter Sunday: Three-Service Production
summary: Coordinated three consecutive services with separate production plans and 22 scheduled media assignments.
facts: 3 services
22 scheduled positions
Run-of-show documentation
fullCaseHtml:
On April 20, 2025, Pentecostal Tabernacle held three Easter Sunday services at its South campus in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Each service required live production, timed speaker and worship transitions, photography, audio, on-screen graphics, and reliable coordination between technical and platform teams.

I prepared the individual call sheets and run-of-show documents and served as producer and technical director, including switching the live program feed for the later services. The work called for one consistent production standard across three consecutive services, while accommodating different staffing, stage elements, and speakers.

Three services, three crew plans

9:00AM SERVICE · 6 MEDIA ASSIGNMENTS

10:30AM SERVICE · 7 MEDIA ASSIGNMENTS

12:00PM SERVICE · 9 MEDIA ASSIGNMENTS

The 22 assignments were planned across three services; volunteers could serve more than one service, so this is not a count of 22 unique people.

Each run of show documented role coverage, individual call times, audio checks, rehearsal and huddle windows, graphics cues, stage transitions, and planned livestream elements. The documents specified which crew members would operate cameras, switching, graphics, front-of-house and livestream audio, and photography.

My challenge was to balance operational precision with the practical reality of running several events in sequence. The second and third productions began with much shorter setup windows than the first.

Designing the operating plan

RECONSTRUCTED PRODUCTION CHECKLISTAPR 20 · 2025

Before doors

Production crew setup, microphone testing, camera checks, audio soundcheck, and graphics playlist preparation.

Before each service

Confirm staff positions, call times, the team huddle, the livestream countdown, and speaker handoffs.

During the program

Coordinate worship, speakers, offering video, lower thirds, lyrics, lighting states, and recording.

Between services

Reset and check media, brief the next presenter, confirm camera and graphics coverage, and transition the team.

Recreated from the three working run-of-show documents. Names, phone numbers, and private internal links have been omitted.

A production built around cues

The original 9:00 AM plan began early with equipment setup, separate soundcheck and media-check windows, a pre-service huddle, and countdown content. The later run-of-show versions covered the distinct camera positions and graphics staff available at 10:30 AM and noon.

These weren't just schedules. They were shared operational documents connecting the live visual output with the audio, stage, worship, and speaking teams. They made it possible to assign tasks in advance, explain what came next, and respond when a service moved faster or slower than expected.

What this demonstrates

  • Technical direction: Operated and coordinated the live video program, including switching, graphics, and media playback.

  • Production management: Prepared three separate run-of-show documents rather than using a generic event template.

  • Team coordination: Built coverage plans for 22 assignments across six, seven, and nine positions per service.

  • Communication: Distributed call times and department cues to help audio, worship, media, and stage teams work in sync.

In response to the Easter run-of-show plans, a PT leadership member sent this feedback:

I want you to know how much I appreciate the excellent job you’ve been doing. It is a blessing that PT’s services have maintained excellence. — Elder Roy M. Ray Jr., April 18, 2025

That feedback was meaningful because it acknowledged work that most audiences never see: the preparation required for a demanding service schedule.

This project represents a part of creative leadership that isn't always visible in the finished livestream: the preparation and people coordination that make complex live events possible.

title: In His Presence: Live Album Proposal
summary: A creative strategy proposal to develop an album from existing live-event recordings; not a released album.

fullCaseHtml:
A major live music event can have a life beyond the night itself. After Pentecostal Tabernacle's 2024 Worship Night, I proposed developing a live album from the performances captured during the event.

In November 2024, I wrote and shared a proposal titled In His Presence, asking PT's creative leadership to consider releasing the songs as a recorded project.

The strategic idea

The opportunity was to turn an event-based production into a lasting audio product: a set of recordings the community could revisit and share beyond the livestream.

Moving from a live recording to an album also raised practical questions. The concept needed to be evaluated with the people responsible for worship, production, mixing, and distribution before it could become a release.

01Identify the assetLive worship recordings captured during a significant event.

02Make the casePitch a focused album concept and invite leadership review.

03Scope feasibilityExplore the mixing and production resources needed for a potential release.

What the record confirms

  • November 22, 2024: I distributed the formal album proposal to PT leadership.

  • November 22–27: The concept received encouraging feedback and was referred for further discussion.

  • January 14, 2025: An assigned follow-up task referenced obtaining mixing numbers for the WN 24 Live Album.

These records establish the idea, my authorship of the proposal, leadership interest, and an initial follow-up step. They do not establish that the album was completed or commercially released, so this case study is presented as a strategic concept rather than a published album.

Open original proposal (PDF) ↗

Original proposal is a high-resolution PDF hosted in Google Drive and may take longer to open.

Why it belongs in my portfolio

This work reflects my interest in creative leadership beyond executing assigned tasks. I looked at an event we had already produced, identified an opportunity for additional storytelling and distribution, prepared a proposal, and initiated discussion about what production would require.

It is an example of taking initiative, articulating a creative opportunity, and connecting media production to a longer-term content strategy.

title: Some Sweet Day — Original Music for Documentary
org: ant/honey · A film by Rasheed Peters
summary: Original music for a 19-minute documentary about grief and memory, evolved from the Dead Yard installation.
facts: Original music credited to Bethel Adekogbe and Shelice Brown-Sanni
19:36 experimental documentary completed in 2023; presented in 2024
Six official festival/program selections, including Black Harvest, Windrush and Conch Shell
Developed from the earlier Dead Yard documentary installation
mediaNote: Square-safe promotional art and the original portrait film poster. Full credits and trailer are in the case study.
fullCaseHtml:
Some Sweet Day is a 19-minute, 36-second experimental personal documentary directed by Rasheed Peters. Following Peters and his mother, Camille, after the death of his father, Owen Anthony Peters, the film explores grief, difficult emotions, regret, and the ways family memories endure. Filmed between Jamaica and the United States, it brings together an intimate mother-and-son conversation, family photographs, wedding footage, and funeral footage.

My contribution: original music

I am credited for original music, alongside Shelice Brown-Sanni. This film grew from Dead Yard, the four-channel installation for which I produced, composed, recorded, arranged, mixed, and mastered the accompanying EP. That earlier work used music informed by Jamaican mourning songs and hymns to support the installation's story of loss and remembrance.

Some Sweet Day carries that creative collaboration into a distinct cinematic form. I am presenting my contribution here specifically as original music for the film, not as film direction, picture editing, or final film sound mixing. The film's official EPK credits Ye Xi with sound design and mix.

Explore the earlier Dead Yard music-production project ↗Listen to the Dead Yard EP ↗

Watch the official trailer

Watch the trailer on Vimeo ↗Official film page — Rasheed Peters ↗

How the film developed

Rasheed Peters's director's statement explains that the original project began as an exploration of anticipatory grief during his father's long illness. After his father's passing in 2022, Peters created Dead Yard (2023), an immersive installation drawing on Jamaican mourning traditions and family stories. The project later evolved into Some Sweet Day, a more intimate, single-screen documentary focused on his mother's experiences as a grieving wife and parent.

The film was completed October 2, 2023; the creator's official film page identifies it as a 2024 short documentary. The distinction matters: 2023 is the completion year, while 2024 is the year of its prominent festival presentations.

Festival and screening selections

The film's FilmFreeway screening record documents six official selections:

  • Chicago Filmmakers — SEEN, Volume 17

  • Iowa City International Documentary Festival

  • Windrush Caribbean Film Festival

  • Conch Shell International Film Festival — 2024 New York City premiere, according to the festival organizer

  • Full Spectrum Features — Our Right to Gaze

  • Black Harvest Film Festival

These are festival or screening selections, not award wins.

Film credits

  • Director, producer, cinematography: Rasheed Peters

  • Editor and film sound design/mix: Ye Xi (also credited as Xi Ye in the FilmFreeway materials)

  • Story editor: Maya Wanner

  • Original music: Bethel Adekogbe and Shelice Brown-Sanni

  • Color and graphics: Ella Harmon (EPK credit); Eleanor Harmon (FilmFreeway listing)

  • Featured: Camille Peters

The film is dedicated to the memory of Owen Anthony Peters.

title: Dead Yard — Music Production & Sound
org: Dead Yard · A project by Rasheed Peters
role: Music Producer · Composer · Recording Engineer · Mixing & Mastering Engineer
summary: Complete music production for the Dead Yard EP and Rasheed Peters's immersive documentary installation.
facts: Composed and produced beats; recorded all instrumental performances
Engineered the vocal recording sessions in my studio with Shelice Brown-Sanni and Savio (Justin Jimenez)
Arranged, mixed, and mastered the EP
Presented as part of Northwestern University's Documentary Media MFA Showcase on June 9, 2023
mediaNote: Original Dead Yard EP artwork and documentary installation photographs.
fullCaseHtml:
Dead Yard is a four-channel experimental documentary installation created by Rasheed Peters as a living memorial to his father. Inspired by the Jamaican tradition of the dead yard—a communal gathering for mourning, remembrance, prayer, storytelling, and music—the project brings together documentary footage, family archives, sound, and memorial objects. The work explores how cultural rituals and grief are experienced when migration separates people from their communities.

My contribution

I led the complete music-production process for the accompanying Dead Yard EP, from composing and producing the beats to recording all instrumental performances, arranging the songs, engineering the vocal sessions in my studio, and completing the final mixes and masters.

I collaborated with vocalists Shelice Brown-Sanni and Savio (Justin Jimenez) to reinterpret traditional Jamaican mourning songs, hymns, and nine-night music through contemporary arrangements and textures. The resulting recordings were released as an EP and formed an integral part of the installation's sonic experience.

Music and installation

The musical score connects the work's spiritual, cultural, and familial themes. In Rasheed Peters's description of the installation, familiar hymns and mourning songs are reshaped through arrangements and textures to evoke the shifting experiences of memory, mourning, and home. The installation combines the music with environmental sounds such as birds, fire, voices, and silence.

Listen to the EP

Listen to the Dead Yard EP on SoundCloud ↗Explore Rasheed Peters's installation ↗

Inside the installation

From Dead Yard to Some Sweet Day

The documentary material from Rasheed Peters's Dead Yard installation later evolved into Some Sweet Day, a 19-minute, 36-second experimental documentary focusing on the filmmaker and his mother, Camille, after the death of his father. The film was completed in 2023 and presented in 2024.

I am credited for original music on the film alongside Shelice Brown-Sanni, building on the preceding EP production. These are distinct credits: I produced, recorded, arranged, mixed, and mastered the Dead Yard EP; Ye Xi is credited for the finished film's sound design and mix. The documentary received six official festival or program selections, including Black Harvest, Windrush Caribbean, and Conch Shell International.

Explore Some Sweet Day in this portfolio ↗Watch the documentary trailer ↗Official film page ↗

Exhibition

Dead Yard was presented on June 9, 2023, as part of Northwestern University's Documentary Media MFA Showcase. It appeared in Binding Domains, a showcase presentation alongside Laura Gede's Passive Transport. Marquise Mays's contemporary review also describes the installation in Northwestern University's Abbot Hall.

Credits

  • Project creator / installation: Rasheed Peters

  • Music production, composition, instrumental recording, arrangement, vocal recording engineering, mixing and mastering: Bethel Adekogbe

  • Vocalists: Shelice Brown-Sanni and Savio (Justin Jimenez)

role: Technical Director · Video Editor · Music Producer · Audio Engineer

Original music for the intro and episodes
First-cut edits and social promotions on weekly deadlines
mediaNote: Official photographs from Proper Bantah; individual photographer credits to be confirmed.
fullCaseHtml:
Proper Bantah is a talk show created by Rasheed Peters in 2018 to give people a place to tell their stories while offering entertaining, accessible inspiration. It premiered at Brandeis University on January 18, 2019.

As Technical Director, I worked across filming and post-production. I operated cameras, recorded interview audio, and helped set up and break down each shoot. I also cleaned up episode audio and created all of the show's original music, including its intro and background tracks.

I edited alongside the team on the full interviews, often putting together first cuts so other editors could focus on clean-up and final revisions. With most of us balancing classes and other jobs, that teamwork was essential to meeting our weekly deadlines.

I had full creative control over the promotional videos: choosing interesting interview moments, pulling funny clips from the in the field segments, and making horizontal and vertical edits with graphics and captions. One of my favorites was the Jonathan Goldman interview. We played indoor racquetball for his field segment, and I turned the footage into an ESPN-style highlight reel for the episode intro and promotion.

Our videos encouraged people to watch the show and attend in-person tapings. Across Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, the show reached more than 7,500 combined views (reported).

fullCaseHtml:
Lakeside's Treasure (2023) is a short documentary directed by Rasheed Peters about Betty McDaniel, whose Lakeside Treasures antique and vintage shop in Chicago's Rogers Park neighborhood grew from a post-retirement dream into a lasting community fixture. Rather than treating the shop simply as a collection of objects, the film centers the dedication, independence, and personal history behind it.

My contribution — original soundtrack

I composed the entire soundtrack for the documentary, creating the music heard throughout the finished film. My responsibility was the film's original music, while direction and filmmaking are credited to Rasheed Peters. This project demonstrates composing music to support a nonfiction narrative, with the soundtrack serving the film's images, dialogue, and portrait of Betty McDaniel.

Watch the documentary

Watch the 9-minute film via the public YouTube release ↗.

The story and release

The documentary follows Betty McDaniel's enthusiasm for the antiques and vintage items she curates and the place her store holds in the surrounding neighborhood. The Chicago Crusader described the film as a portrait of a woman continuing to pursue her ambitions after retirement.

Lakeside's Treasure premiered on September 18, 2023, as Episode 8 of Black Public Media's AfroPoP Digital Shorts. Black Public Media lists its runtime as 9 minutes, 8 seconds. Its release was covered by Chicago's Crusader newspaper.

  • Subject: Betty McDaniel, Lakeside Treasures, Rogers Park, Chicago

  • Release: Black Public Media — AfroPoP Digital Shorts, Episode 8 (2023)

My music collaborations with Rasheed Peters also include Dead Yard and Some Sweet Day. These are separate projects with distinct musical contributions.

Delivered four requested cues and an additional option, mapped to a working cut
mediaNote: Official Creature Feature Heart Eater film poster, seven production stills, and archival score materials. My role: original music composer.
fullCaseHtml:
Creature Feature Heart Eater is a 2022 fantasy, romance, and dramedy short film with horror elements, directed by Guinevere Thomas in the American Film Institute production context. I was invited to compose original music for its romantic, dramatic, transformation, and suspense sequences.

Official film poster (2022).

Film synopsis

Maggie has denounced love after a particularly gruesome high school break-up, finds herself tangled up in love's web once more. Now she must find a way to pursue her feelings while keeping her inner demons at bay. Will she succeed this time?

Scene from Creature Feature Heart Eater (2022).

Developing the musical language

  • Kylie's Corsage — first transformation / horror

  • Montage Song — romantic montage slot

  • Graveyard / Graveyard Woes — later transformation and graveyard / horror

  • Blah Blah Blah — closing sequence

  • Lovers — additional musical option

  • Heartbreak Harper — introductory cue title referenced during revisions

These are names and scene assignments from my working cue sheet and email correspondence. Not every alternative is necessarily part of the finished soundtrack.

Revision and collaboration

After delivering the initial score package on February 22, 2022, I revised the music to better match feedback and the editor's needs. This included separating an introduction from a horror cue, producing different intensity versions, and trying a stronger graveyard treatment. I also shared commercial-song references as possible editorial directions for a romantic montage; those references should not be confused with my own compositions.

I sent further revisions on February 25, February 27, and March 4. The surviving emails, score notes, and original music archive document a collaborative process of writing to picture, delivering options, and refining dramatic impact.
